title: American shoppers are taking a breather ahead of the holiday season | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

Americans reined in some purchases last month – particularly the more expensive items such as cars and furniture – logging the weakest retail sales gain in three months, new data showed Tuesday.

US retail sales rose 0.2% in October, a slowdown after gas prices drove a 0.8% gain the month before, according to Commerce Department data.

Economists say the overall pullback, however, masks underlying strength of a resilient American consumer who also very well could be gearing up for the holiday shopping season.

“The US consumer looks solid and is bending, not breaking, under the weight of higher energy prices,” Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, told CNN. “We know that higher inflation is hurting consumers, but I think that’s just been offset by the strengthening in the labor market we’ve seen this year.”

October’s spending tally was driven lower by a drop in car sales that offset a more modest uptick in gasoline station sales (which slowed to a gain of 1.5% versus a 6% increase in September as fuel prices softened a bit after surging higher the two months prior).

Retail sales are adjusted for seasonal swings but not inflation, which rose 0.4% in October, Consumer Price Index data shows.

In addition to falling sales of cars, Tuesday report showed consumers spent less on furniture, sporting goods and apparel; and also cut back on their purchases at the grocery store.

“Conversely, grocery sales declined, which in a nominal report reflects a notable pullback in volume as food inflation outpaces spending,” said Mike Reid, head of US economics for RBC. “But, the weakness there is overshadowed by the strength elsewhere, as upper income households continue to drive consumption.”

The pullback on bigger-ticket purchases in October could be an indication that consumers are gearing up for the holiday shopping season, said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360.

“Several of the categories where spending declined are discretionary categories – purchases you can put off for a while because you don’t need those goods every single month,” she wrote in a note Tuesday. “Because this is October data, savvy families may be saving those purchases for holiday sale deals.”

To be sure, a closely watched category of spending that strips out some more volatile areas (such as gasoline stations, auto sales, building materials and restaurants) rose at a stronger-than-expected rate of 0.6%, a tick higher than a 0.5% gain notched in September.

Sales at miscellaneous stores (a catch-all category that includes retailers in pet supplies, office goods, florists, Halloween costumes, etc.) saw the biggest gains in October, at 4.7%, while spending remained firm at health and personal care stores as well as online retailers (Amazon, for example, held a sales event early last month).

Tuesday’s report underscored the ongoing bifurcation of household finances, ING chief international economist James Knightley said, noting the differing trajectories of spending among high-income individuals versus middle- and lower-income Americans.

“Middle- and lower-income households tend to spend more of their income of physical goods, such as food and clothing, and squeezed spending power limits the potential for growth,” he wrote. “Conversely, high income households have seen their wealth surge, boosting consumption, and are accounting for a growing share of total consumer spending.”

In addition to Tuesday’s retail sales data, a fuller picture of consumer health and spending could come via Target and Walmart, which are slated to release their latest earnings reports on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively, this week.

Consumers appear to still have an appetite to spend but are being picky about what they’re buying, EY-Parthenon economists wrote Tuesday.

“Cost-of-living concerns were front and center in the midterm elections and underscored the lasting imprint of accumulated inflation on household finances,” wrote economists Gregory Daco and Lydia Boussour. “While consumers still have the capacity to spend, it should not be confused with comfort.”
